1.pericope_label: After this opened Job his mouth, and cursed his day. And Job spake, and said,

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch treat the second verse as a problem in accentuation, three words separated so as to force an unusual pointing on the verb, and gloss it as beginning to speak on some previous incitement rather than replying to anything; they report the division modern critics make of the speech, a delirious cursing of life, an eager longing for death, and a reproachful inquiry after the end of such a life, then deny these are strophes at all while refusing the further claim that the book has no strophic structure anywhere. Ellicott raises a question of priority none of the others touch: the resemblance between this chapter and a lament in Jeremiah is so close that one must be borrowed from the other, and he holds this the original, since the chapter is indispensable to the poem here while in the prophet it occurs casually, as the record of a passing mood, and reads like a man quoting a familiar writing much as he might quote a psalm.

Gill reads the opening phrase as the breaking of a long silence, Job having spoken after the first trial to bless the name of the Lord and after the second to reprove his wife, but saying nothing through the seven days until he saw that his friends would not speak either. He notes that the second verse says answered although nobody had spoken to him, and takes it with one commentator that Job answered his own calamity and their silence while an older authority renders it that he cried out; he agrees that the metre begins here but is candid that the metre itself is now pretty much unknown even to the Jews, reports the opinion that the speeches were not delivered in verse but put into that form afterwards by the writer, and adds that one Targum has not that Job spoke but that he sang.

Clarke draws the line of the poetry here and defends it: there is nothing in the preceding chapters either in the form or the spirit of Hebrew poetry, and though it is easy to break narrative into half-lines that does not make it verse, Asiatic poets commonly opening with prose and only then beginning the poem. He grants his opponents their opinion in a sentence that concedes nothing, that they have his consent while he takes the liberty of believing most decidedly the opposite. Wesley refuses to excuse the curse, since Job is afterwards reproved by God and accuses himself; he allows that Job stops short of cursing God and so makes the devil a liar, but holds that he reflects on providence indirectly, and calls the curse sinful on two counts, that it was vain, being spent on a thing incapable of blessing or cursing, and that it laid blame on God for giving him life that day.

Henry makes the silence itself the cause of what follows: Job's heart had long been hot within him, and while he was musing the fire burned, and burned the more for being stifled. The friends were afraid to speak lest they grieve him and he lest he offend them; they had come to comfort him but, finding his affliction so far out of the common, began to suspect him a hypocrite and to think comfort did not belong to him. Losers, Henry adds drily, think they may have leave to speak. He allows that the extremity of the trouble may excuse the curse in part, and observes that where other men keep their birthday with rejoicing this man reckoned it the unhappiest day of his year, being the inlet to all his woe.

debates.question: Can Job's curse on his day be excused?

positions.position: In part, by the extremity of the trouble and the disorder of his spirits
Not at all: God afterwards reproves him and he accuses himself, and the curse was both vain and a reflection on providence

debates.question: Where does the poetry of the book begin?

positions.position: Here and decidedly, since nothing in the earlier chapters has either the form or the spirit of Hebrew poetry
Here, though the metre is now unknown, and the speeches may have been put into verse afterwards by the writer
Here, but the divisions modern critics make of the speech are not strophes, whatever may be said of the book elsewhere

outliers.claim: Argues that this chapter is the original and the parallel lament in Jeremiah the borrowing, since the chapter is indispensable to the poem here while in the prophet it occurs casually as a passing mood.
Reports that one Targum renders the verb not that Job spoke but that he sang.

themes: After this opened Job his mouth, and cursed his day.

3.pericope_label: Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived. Let that day be darkness; let not God regard it from above, neither let the light shine upon it. Let darkness and the shadow of death stain it; let a cloud dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it. As for that night, let darkness seize upon it; let it not be joined unto the days of the year, let it not come into the number of the months. Lo, let that night be solitary, let no joyful voice come therein. Let them curse it that curse the day, who are ready to raise up their mourning. Let the stars of the twilight thereof be dark; let it look for light, but have none; neither let it see the dawning of the day: Because it shut not up the doors of my mother’s womb, nor hid sorrow from mine eyes.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch decide against a named opponent that the curse falls on the birth-day and the night of conception as they recur yearly, not on the actual first day. Ellicott takes the disputed verb literally as redeem, so that darkness and the shadow of death claim the day as their rightful inheritance; on the night he prefers let it not rejoice among the days of the year, as one of a glorious procession of nights, supplies the phrase the eyelids of the dawn, and offers the reading of the hardest verse that Clarke could not find, that those who pronounce days unlucky should treat this one as the standard, noting that they are further described as ready to rouse leviathan, which is to say as desperate as that.

Gill allows both readings of what is cursed, the identical day on which Job was born, which amounts to wishing he had never been born, or the birthday as it came round yearly; on the first the wish is impossible and Job knew it, the design being to show the greatness of the affliction rather than to obtain anything. He is explicit that the darkness asked for is not the figurative darkness of calamity but gross natural darkness, reports the rendering by which darkness and the shadow of death redeem the day, claiming it as their own and leaving light no share in it, and fills in what a solitary night lacks, the journeys and business, the meetings of friends after the day's work, the feasts usual at night and at marriages.

Clarke settles a smaller point the same way as Keil and Delitzsch, that though the word properly means conceived it should here be taken of birth, since it is most unlikely that the night of conception should be known or published. He reduces the imprecation to a phrase, that the day be blotted out of the calendar, and sharpens it by remembering what the day had been, the birthday of a man once celebrated for his possessions and piety; on the disputed verb he goes instead to the root that gives the kinsman-redeemer, whose office was to buy back an inheritance and avenge a death, and makes the sense pursuit rather than possession. The word rendered solitary he traces to Arabic, from a root meaning to cut off or lay bare which also yields words for a rock and a burden, glossing it that the night should be as destitute of good as a bare rock is of verdure; and of the verse about those who curse the day he says the English is scarcely intelligible and that he has waded through many interpretations without arriving at a probable notion. Wesley makes the observation that governs the passage, that sense is ascribed to the night by a poetical fiction usual in all writers, and keeps the hard verse simple, that men cursing their own birthday should spare a curse for Job's.

positions.position: Either the identical day of birth, which is to wish he had never been born, or the anniversary as it returns
The anniversary only: the birth-day and the night of conception as they recur yearly, not the actual first day

positions.position: Literally redeem, darkness and the shadow of death claiming the day as their rightful inheritance
From the root of the avenger of blood, so that the day is pursued and overtaken rather than possessed

outliers.claim: Admits that the verse about those who curse the day is scarcely intelligible in English and that he has found no probable notion of it, rejecting the usual appeal to professional cursers as unworthy of a man who knew God's government as Job did.
Supplies the reading Clarke could not find, that those who pronounce days unlucky should take this one as their standard, and notes that they are described as ready to rouse leviathan.

11.pericope_label: Why died I not from the womb? why did I not give up the ghost when I came out of the belly? Why did the knees prevent me? or why the breasts that I should suck? For now should I have lain still and been quiet, I should have slept: then had I been at rest, With kings and counsellors of the earth, which built desolate places for themselves; Or with princes that had gold, who filled their houses with silver:

schools.summary: Ellicott puts the complaint about the knees in one sentence, asking why Job was nursed with care instead of being allowed to fall to the ground and be killed; on the desolate places he sharpens the paradox, that gorgeous tombs are desolate precisely because none but the dead tenant them, though he allows the other sense, that places built of old now lie ruined, and thinks the pyramids may be hinted at in the first. Keil and Delitzsch state the principle the passage turns on, that there all enjoy the rest they could not find here, the troublers and the troubled alike.

Gill presses the first of the three wishes, that since conception was not prevented Job wishes at least to have died before coming out alive; he identifies the knees as the midwife's rather than the mother's, or possibly the father's, since it was the custom to take a newborn on the knee in acknowledgement, so that the complaint is that Job was caught instead of left to fall. He makes the grave to the dead what a bed is to the living, a place of ease free from care and thought and better than a bed since on a bed there is often tossing to and fro, offers first that Job might have been buried with kings as his own ancestors, then prefers the levelling sense that death spares neither the power of kings nor the wisdom of counsellors and that after it a child who died at birth stands equal with them, and notes of the princes that their riches lay in metal rather than dominion and could not preserve them from death.

Clarke separates three wishes where the English runs them together, dying in the womb without coming to maturity, being born dead without drawing breath, and dying shortly after birth, and holds that all three are meant. He defines the counsellors as the privy advisers without whom kings seldom undertake wars, observes that these great agitators of the world, most of them troublers of its peace, are now at rest, takes the desolate places for mausoleums and sepulchral pyramids raised to keep a name from perishing while the body turns to corruption, and lets the princes keep only the empty places prepared for a last dwelling, closing with a saying from an eastern writer that nothing satisfies the covetous but the dust that fills his mouth in the grave. Wesley expands the complaint about the knees and then turns on it: the nurse's laying him there rather than on the bare ground is what he calls their cruel kindness, and he records his verdict that Job is here unthankfully despising the wonderful mercies of God toward helpless infants. On the desolate places he reads the line differently from the others, of men who to show their wealth or leave a glorious name rebuilt ruined cities, or built new cities and palaces where before there was only solitude and waste.

Henry watches the argument rather than the grammar and dislikes where it goes. Job, reflecting on the folly of wishing he had never been born, tries to mend it with something little better; and though a saying about the barren womb is allowed elsewhere, blessing the barren womb is one thing and cursing the fruitful womb another. His rule is brief: it is good to make the best of afflictions, but not to make the worst of mercies.

debates.question: What are the desolate places that kings built for themselves?

positions.position: Tombs: mausoleums and sepulchral pyramids raised to keep a name from perishing while the body corrupts
Cities: ruined ones rebuilt, or new cities and palaces raised where before there was only solitude and waste

outliers.claim: Calls the nurse's catching of the newborn their cruel kindness and delivers his own verdict against Job, that he is here unthankfully despising the mercies of God toward helpless infants.
Answers the wish with a rule of proportion, that it is good to make the best of afflictions but not to make the worst of mercies.

16.pericope_label: Or as an hidden untimely birth I had not been; as infants which never saw light. There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest. There the prisoners rest together; they hear not the voice of the oppressor. The small and great are there; and the servant is free from his master.

schools.summary: Ellicott passes over the detail of the untimely birth and states only what the condition would have secured, a release from the experience of suffering; he supplies the one thing the verse about the wicked leaves unsaid, that there means in the grave, the place indicated but never distinctly expressed, and notices with Clarke that the word for the oppressor is the one rendered taskmaster in the account of the Egyptian bondage. Keil and Delitzsch render the line about the prisoners differently again, that the captives dwell together in tranquillity and do not hear the voice of the taskmaster.

Gill notes that the word for the untimely birth carries the sense of falling, an abortive being like fruit that drops before it ripens, and that it is called hidden either as hidden in the belly, on one old rendering, or as hidden from sight, having come to no proper shape. He takes the troublers to be men like the troubled sea that cannot rest, and names three kinds who trouble good men in particular, profane persons by their lives, false teachers by their doctrines, and persecutors by their hard speeches; in the grave there is neither work nor device, so that men who could not sleep unless they had done mischief now have no power to do any. On the prisoners he thinks of men held for debt, condemned to the galleys, or in bonds for religion, and makes the point that at death the chains are knocked off and they rest not only with their fellow prisoners but with the men who put them there; and the levelling of small and great he takes to cover age and stature and estate together.

Clarke distinguishes two cases in the verse about the untimely birth, an early miscarriage scarcely perceptible to the mother, in which the child never had the distinguishable form of a human being, and the infants named next, farther advanced but lost long before their time. He reads the verse about the wicked as a pair of opposites deliberately set against each other, the troubles and the troubled, the restless and the submissive, the toils of the great and the labours of the slave; describes slaves who felt all the troubles of life and scarcely tasted its pleasures, and says the voice of the oppressor, more terrible to them than death, is heard no more. He calls the grave the appointed place of rendezvous where all these travellers meet, and draws the moral from the shape of a life rather than its end, that equality is absolute at the entrance and the exit while the whole intermediate state is disparity, so that the thought should humble the great and small alike. Wesley names the oppressors' works as vexations and rapines and murders, observes that those tired out by them now sleep quietly beside them, and turns the levelling into two practical rules, that those who have power should use it moderately and those in subjection bear it patiently. He also sets the limit that keeps the passage honest, that Job is not treating of the state of the dead hereafter, of which he speaks later, but only of their freedom from the troubles of this world.

outliers.claim: Limits the passage against a natural misreading, holding that Job is not treating here of the state of the dead hereafter but only of their freedom from the troubles of this world.
Draws the moral from the shape of a life rather than its end: equality is absolute at the entrance and the exit, and the whole intermediate state is disparity.
Presses the reunion the grave makes, where prisoners rest not only with their fellow prisoners but with the men who put them there.

20.pericope_label: Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter in soul; Which long for death, but it cometh not; and dig for it more than for hid treasures; Which rejoice exceedingly, and are glad, when they can find the grave? Why is light given to a man whose way is hid, and whom God hath hedged in?

schools.summary: Ellicott points to the older connection between life and light elsewhere in Scripture, and then adds the one thing that changes the colour of the verse about the hedge: this is the same expression used earlier in the book in exactly the opposite sense, where the hedge about the man was why the adversary could not touch him.

Gill takes the light for the light of the living, sweet to a man in health and not to one in pain of body and anguish of mind, who would rather be in the silent grave; he piles up the verbs of longing, that such men desire and gape for death as a hungry man for his food, and gives the reason it does not come, that the fixed time is not yet, adding the caution that death is not desirable in itself, being a dissolution of nature and the wages of sin, though good men may lawfully desire it to be free from sinning. The man whose way is hidden he applies to Job directly, whose way, as he complains, was hidden from the Lord and overlooked, with no regard had to the injuries done him.

Clarke puts the complaint as a question about fitness, why life is granted to a man incapable of enjoying it or of performing its functions, and measures the longing by comparison, that such men desire separation from life more than men who love gold desire a rich mine; he reports a manuscript variant which, by the change of a single letter, turns rejoicing with joy into rejoicing at the tomb. On the man whose way is hidden he takes him for one who knows nothing of what lies before him and is full of fears about both worlds, points to an exact parallel in the Lamentations where the same complaint is made of being hedged about and the ways enclosed with hewn stone, and declines a conjectural rendering since the common text yields an easy sense already. Wesley makes two observations that pull against each other and keeps both: a defence, that however earnestly Job dug after death he never did anything to hasten it but was content to wait all the days of his appointed time; and a rebuke, that impatience of life on account of its troubles is unnatural and ungrateful to the giver of life. He also explains why life is called light, since light is pleasant and serviceable for walking and working, and why it is said to be given, since it would be lost were it not daily renewed by a fresh gift.

Henry reads the verse for what it does not say. The Hebrew runs why doth he give light, without a subject, and he observes that Job means God and will not name him, setting this against the adversary's prediction that the man would curse God to his face. He is not indulgent about the rest: when men are set on quarrelling there is no end of it, and the corrupt heart will carry on the humour; having cursed the day of his birth Job now courts the day of his death, and the beginning of such impatience is as the letting forth of water. Bitterness of soul, he adds, makes life itself bitter.

outliers.claim: Observes that the hedge Job complains of is described with the very expression used earlier in the book for his protection, where the hedge was the reason the adversary could not touch him.

Notices that the Hebrew asks why doth he give light without naming a subject, so that Job means God and will not name him, which Henry sets against the adversary's prediction that he would curse God to his face.
Keeps a defence and a rebuke together, that Job never did anything to hasten his own death and yet that impatience of life on account of its troubles is ungrateful to the giver of life.

themes: Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter in soul;
Which long for death, but it cometh not; and dig for it more than for hid treasures;

24.pericope_label: For my sighing cometh before I eat, and my roarings are poured out like the waters. For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me. I was not in safety, neither had I rest, neither was I quiet; yet trouble came.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch reach Clarke's preferred sense by the preposition, rendering the line that instead of his food his sighing comes, and noting that the word passes from a local meaning to a substitutionary one as the Latin does. Ellicott puts the pathos of the admitted fear more sharply than the others: Job had kept the uncertainty of earthly things always in remembrance, and was overtaken all the same by a calamity that mocked his carefulness and went beyond anything he had apprehended.

Gill keeps closer to the surface of the sighing, that there was nothing but sighing before Job sat down and tears mingled with the food while he ate, so that these were his meat and drink continually. On the fear he reports one view that it was for his children, lest they should sin and bring down judgment, and another that it covered all his troubles, which the changeableness of the world had always led him to expect; on either reading the remark justifies the expostulation, since a man who never had pleasure even in his greatest prosperity may well ask why light is continued to him. Of the last verse he argues that it cannot refer to the time of prosperity at all, since Job was then plainly in safety, God having set a hedge about him so that neither his enemies nor the adversary himself could reach him.

Clarke gives two readings of the sighing that comes before food, one attributed to an early commentator, that Job's body was so ulcerated he could neither lift food to his mouth nor chew it, and one he prefers as more natural, that the sighing took away appetite and served him in place of meat; he sets beside it the psalmist whose tears had been his meat day and night and remarks that the resemblance is probably not imitation either way but two men describing the same thing. He compares the roarings to the noise of a murmuring stream, turns Job's admission of prior fear into a defence, that it proves he was not lifted up but knew what he had was from Providence and that the giver might take away, so that he is not being stripped as a punishment for self-confidence, and proposes reading the last verse as a series of questions, which yields an easy sense: was I not in safety, had I not rest, and yet trouble came. He reports a third rendering which makes the point neither past security nor past unrest but speed, the evils treading one upon the heels of another, and compares the psalm where deep calls to deep. Wesley says the roarings were loud outcries more befitting a lion than a man, poured out with abundance and violence like waters that break their banks; he says in the first person that even in prosperity Job was full of fears, considering the variety of God's providences and the instability of this vain world, and takes the last verse as a claim about conduct rather than circumstance, that Job had not misbehaved himself in prosperity by presumption but had walked humbly, from which he concludes that in this respect too the man's way was hidden, since he could not see why God should be contending with him.

debates.question: Does I was not in safety refer to Job's time of prosperity?

positions.position: It cannot, since he was then plainly in safety, God having set a hedge about him that neither his enemies nor the adversary could pass
It does, if the clauses are read as questions: was I not in safety, had I not rest, and yet trouble came
It is a claim about conduct rather than circumstance, that he had not abused prosperity by presumption but walked humbly in it

outliers.claim: Sharpens the pathos of the admitted fear, that Job had kept the instability of earthly things always in remembrance and was overtaken all the same by a calamity that mocked his carefulness.
Turns the admission of prior fear into a defence, since it proves Job was not lifted up but knew the giver might take away, so that he is not being stripped as a punishment for self-confidence.
